Such facilities were believed to be essential to sustaining America’s effort in science. The construction and operation of large-scale scientific user facilities have been integral to the mission of the DOE Office of Science from the earliest days. Today, we maintain and operate 28 DOE Office of Science user facilities at DOE national laboratories across the country as shared resources for the scientific community, with access determined on a competitive basis using peer review. pages.text: Oficina de Normas de Gestión Laboral | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Oficina de Normas de Gestión Laboral La Oficina de Normas de Gestión Laboral (Office of Labor-Management Standards, u OLMS, por sus siglas en inglés) pertenece al Departamento de Trabajo de los Estados Unidos y es responsable de administrar y aplicar la mayoría de las disposiciones de la Ley de Notificación y Divulgación Gestión Laboral (Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act, o LMRDA, por sus siglas en inglés). Dicha ley fue adoptada con el fin de garantizar normas básicas de democracia y responsabilidad fiscal en las organizaciones laborales del sector privado. Los sindicatos que representan a los empleados del Correo Postal de los Estados Unidos también se hallan sujetos a la LMRDA. Los sindicatos de empleados federales se hallan sujetos a normas similares conforme a la Ley de Reforma del Servicio Civil de 1978 (Civil Service Reform Act, o CSRA, por sus siglas in inglés) y a la Ley del Servicio Exterior de 1980. La OLMS anima a que los oficiales y los miembros del sindicato, así como otros individuos afectados por la LMRDA, se pongan en contacto con la agencia para discutir de problemas, presenten quejas u obtengan información sobre la LMRDA. Además, la OLMS fomenta la conformidad voluntaria con la LMRDA al informar a oficiales del sindicato y a otros individuos de sus responsabilidades y al animar a los miembros del sindicato a que ejerzan sus derechos. Photograph: AP Oklahoma This article is more than 6 months old Oklahoma’s Richard Glossip freed on bond after 30 years on death row This article is more than 6 months old A judge set a $500,000 bond in the 1997 murder case headed for retrial after a supreme court decision Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email Associated Press Thu 14 May 2026 13.50 EDT Last modified on Thu 14 May 2026 14.07 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An Oklahoma judge on Thursday allowed Richard Glossip, a former death row prisoner, to be released on bond after almost 30 years behind bars, as he awaits a retrial over a 1997 killing that put him on the brink of execution three separate times. The decision clears the way for Glossip, 63, to leave prison for the first time since his arrest nearly three decades ago. Last year, the US supreme court threw out his conviction. His longstanding claims of innocence have drawn support from Kim Kardashian and other prominent figures. Natalie Mai, the judge, issued an order setting bond at $500,000. Glossip must wear an electronic monitoring device and will not be allowed to travel outside Oklahoma . He also must not contact any witnesses

The economic downturn, shifting perceptions of retirement, increased workplace flexibility, and the aging of the "baby boom" generation are all contributing to people working longer. pages.text: Oldest footprints in Saudi Arabia reveal intriguing step in early human migration | National Geographic Of the hundreds of fossil footprints found at the Alathar ancient lake deposit in Saudi Arabia, scientists identified seven that were likely made by members of our own species, Homo sapiens. Photograph by Klint Janulis SCIENCE NEWS Oldest footprints in Saudi Arabia reveal intriguing step in early human migration Animal and human tracks show the lush landscape that may have greeted Homo sapiens as they ventured into new lands more than 100,000 years ago. By Maya Wei-Haas Published September 17, 2020 • 9 min read Small oval depressions—376 in all—are scattered across a patch of dry ground nestled between the dunes of northern Saudi Arabia. At a glance, these pockmarks don't seem particularly impressive, so much so that a team of scientists surveying the region almost passed them by in 2017. But upon further examination, the team realized that the depressions were left by an array of ancient animals, and among them were traces of our own species, Homo sapiens . The discovery of human footprints, if confirmed, would mark the oldest trace of our species yet found in the Arabian Peninsula, which sits at the gateway to early humans’ spread around the world. As described in a new study published in Science Advances , the frozen footfalls preserve a striking snapshot of time some 115,000 years ago, as animals and humans congregated near a shallow lake, perhaps with a shared purpose of slaking thirst and sating hunger. By accessing the OLMS EFS, you can also obtain, work on, or sign and submit an LM form. For more information on registering with EFS, see the Registration Help page . pages.text: Olympics gymnatics: Rhys McClenaghan wins pommel horse gold in Paris - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Rhys McClenaghan let out a huge roar after his routine By Andy Gray BBC Sport NI Journalist at Bercy Arena Published 3 August 2024 Rhys McClenaghan has completed gymnastics' 'Grand Slam' after winning pommel horse gold at the Paris Olympics with a stunning routine. The fourth to perform his routine, the Team Ireland gymnast was flawless as his score of 15.533 edged Kazakhstan's Nariman Kurbanov by just 0.100. The USA's Stephen Nedoroscik was third with 15.200. Team GB's Max Whitlock, who went second, scored a 15.200, just 0.333 down on McClenaghan and had to settle for fourth place. After a flawless run, McClenaghan's coach Luke Carson had his head on his hands just before the dismount. When the Newtownards gymnast landed it, both let out a huge roar and there was an emotional embrace between the pair. There was a nervous wait as the remaining four gymnasts took to the pommel horse, with Nedoroscik going closest while backed by the vocal USA support who had just witnessed Simone Biles win gold in the women's vault final. McClenaghan becomes the fourth athlete from Northern Ireland to win a gold medal at these Olympics. The 25-year-old joins swimmer Daniel Wiffen and GB's Hannah Scott in converting their world titles into Olympic gold. Jack McMillan also won a gold medal after helping Team GB to first place in the 4x200m freestyle. pages.text: Omega-3s are great for your health—but supplements may not be | National Geographic Premium HEALTH Omega-3s are great for your health—but supplements may not be Fish oil can reduce inflammation and lower cardiovascular disease risk. Yet a growing body of research suggests that supplements may not offer those same benefits. Omega-3 fatty acids are an essential nutrient that offer numerous benefits for the gut and can even lower risk of cardiovascular disease and stroke. However, research shows that fish oil—a common omega-3 supplement—may not be as effective as scientists once believed. Photograph by MirageC, Getty Images By Daryl Austin Published March 21, 2025 Science has proven time and again that omega-3 fatty acids, or omega-3s, can be among the most important parts of a well-balanced diet. The studies show that the healthy fats can help lower blood pressure , improve immunity , reduce joint inflammation , support mental health , and even diminish risks of cardiovascular disease and stroke. But most people aren't getting enough. In fact, research shows that some 95 percent of kids aren't meeting the recommended levels of omega-3s in their diet—and about 68 percent of adults aren't either. pages.text: One thing Hollywood gets right about Ancient Rome | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE One thing Hollywood gets right about Ancient Rome Gladiators really were sex symbols—just not in the way one might expect. Gladiators were ancient Roman sex symbols Rebecca Hale, National Geographic By Harry Sidebottom Published July 24, 2026 Hollywood is often criticized for getting history wrong, rarely more so than in films about Rome . One could take issue with the lack of color, whether in the robes that clothe posh-sounding British actors or the statues and other works in marble stripped of their polychromy. In arguably the most famous movie about Rome, Gladiator , inaccuracies abound, from puzzling choices in how the gladiators are armed to the tigers released to endanger the combatants. Credulity is strained even further in the sequel when a naval fight is recreated in the Colosseum (which could not be flooded by the period in which the film is set) and great white sharks devour those who fall into the water.
